changes.before: A model flags four items and three are truly positive. What is its precision?
changes.after: Precision asks how many positive predictions were right.

before: Precision asks: among the examples predicted positive, how many really were positive? It is useful when acting on a false alarm has a cost.
If a filter flags ten messages as spam and eight are actually spam, eight of its ten positive predictions were correct. Its precision on that set is 8/10, or 80%.

Worked example: filter A flags five messages, all spam. Filter B flags ten messages, eight spam. A has 100% precision and B has 80% precision on these predictions. This comparison alone says nothing about how much spam either filter missed.

The denominator is true positives plus false positives: every positive prediction. False negatives are not in that denominator. If there are no positive predictions, the raw ratio is undefined; evaluation tools must state their chosen handling.
Changed situation: A model flags four items and three are truly positive. What is its precision?
Precision uses the positive predictions as its denominator, so the ratio is 3/4.
after: Precision asks: of everything the model called positive, how much really was positive? For a spam filter, it checks how trustworthy its spam flags were.
Divide true positives by all positive predictions. All positive predictions means true positives plus false positives.
The bottom number in the fraction is called the denominator. Here it is 10: all the flagged messages. It is not every message in the dataset.
If nothing was predicted positive, this fraction would divide by zero. The raw precision ratio is then undefined. A report should state how it handles that case.
High precision does not show how much spam was missed. A filter can make very few false alarms while failing to find much of the spam.

after.question: A model flags 4 items. Of those, 3 really are positive. What is its precision?
